posts.cooked:
In real messy coding, for my case with undocumented ERP, local llm needs to dig/map all data for local sse mcp tools. Besides monorepo already has 10+ complex modules in production all SOX compliance.

  • On urgent production patches, until last month, I used to have latest Sonnet doing the job (Sonnet costs me 20-30 bucks every time). Right now GLM Flash (earlier Autoround , now Technigma Native) can handle with full trust by me. Oneshot with full test then release to production within few hours, no mistake.
  • Before GLM, DS v4 or Qwen only do the in Dev and UAT environmens, it would take longtime with many cycles.
  • Development, GLM flash will also take time, most of the time One shot , however sometimes it stuck at complex issue, I can’t call Claude, because it will eat my 500-monthly budget in one day. So,
  • When GLM stuck, I need to find different approach, start Qwen flash next/DeepSeek v4 flash vision to jump in and explore, then go back to GLM.

Before I didn’t pay attention to benchmarks, because we only had qwen3.6 27b or 3.5 122b.

But now many choices on models and stacks, TEB scores are useful in some ways.

  • Example, DS score on planning not stable between benchmarks, yes DS planning needs babysis.
  • Qwen is bit better at planning, however implementation is quite terrible. My orchestrator has strict PDCA, so before closing Qwen FN will always find out that it’s implementation missed something and sent follow up to correct/update. I loose trust on such actions.

In short, GLM flash (especially Technigma Native) is my primary choice as of now. This month I only spent few bucks on Sonnet so far ( to fix Technigma config that I messed😂)
posts.raw:
In real messy coding, for my case with undocumented ERP, local llm needs to dig/map all data for local sse mcp tools. Besides monorepo already has 10+ complex modules in production all SOX compliance.

* On urgent production patches, until last month, I used to have latest Sonnet doing the job (Sonnet costs me 20-30 bucks every time). Right now GLM Flash (earlier Autoround , now Technigma Native) can handle with full trust by me. Oneshot with full test then release to production within few hours, no mistake.
* Before GLM, DS v4 or Qwen only do the in Dev and UAT environmens, it would take longtime with many cycles.
* Development, GLM flash will also take time, most of the time One shot , however sometimes it stuck at complex issue, I can't call Claude, because it will eat my 500-monthly budget in one day. So,
* When GLM stuck, I need to find different approach, start Qwen flash next/DeepSeek v4 flash vision to jump in and explore, then go back to GLM. 

Before I didn't pay attention to benchmarks, because we only had qwen3.6 27b or 3.5 122b. 

But now many choices on models and stacks, TEB scores are useful in some ways. 

* Example, DS score on planning not stable between benchmarks, yes DS planning needs babysis.
* Qwen is bit better at planning, however implementation is quite terrible. My orchestrator has strict PDCA, so before closing Qwen FN will always find out that it's implementation missed something and sent follow up to correct/update. I loose trust on such actions.

In short, GLM flash (especially Technigma Native) is my primary choice as of now. This month I only spent few bucks on Sonnet so far ( to fix Technigma config that I messed😂)

posts.cooked:
I actually started to use OpenAI sub (20) very extensively as I developed a very robust pipeline that ships 90% grade ready code now, cutting meticulous testing and fixing with local model. GLM develops plan, tries to pass it via Mr. Sol’s review, get scolded 3-5 times again and again, gets details right, codes, tries to pass Mr. Sol’s meticulous review of the code, get scolded few times, fixes. And ships surprisingly good product. And this make the cheaper SOTA sub super useful. If I would just use cloud - it would never fit into 200 a month, with majority of work done locally 20 is aplenty.

I believe in the end results are better than if I would just ask Sol to develop a plan and implement it. Developer cannot see own faults easily, need a separate set of eyes. Models are mimicking us so it pay to apply same principles as with humans.

posts.cooked:
I was having periodic crashes with MiaAI TF. Mostly close to OOM despite having 14.5 default reserve eventually it creeps up to 121/122 ram taken and barely responsive but no hang, possible to remove containers. Once in 1-2 days. I have increased reserve to 16.5G and reduced kv cache ram allocation by 2GB too. Cache dropped to 2.1M which is still more than plenty. Was working well.
But booted this morning and it crashed again on prefill. No RAM issue, just non premitted CUDA operation on the worker. Falling back to TAI engine.

posts.cooked: Well. It depends entirely on your tasks. Both TensorFold- and vLLM-versions could not create full application on Nest.js from detailed specification in one shot (even had to go in and manually fine-tune a lot of things after them, explicitly pointing out issues throughout the codebase). I would call them equivalent (fp8-version of the TF and NVFP4 version of vLLM) on context size below 250-300k tokens.

Got it. First of all, I believe the author(s) of the “gr8” repo you referred to is one of our community members, @matthew16 , who recently posted Kindling Spark OS - ~4GB+ free RAM

“gr8 is a from-scratch CUDA inference engine for the full GLM 5.3 model”. It currently does not support “GLM 5.3 Flash”, but there might be some tweaks possible. The idea is very interesting as that X post indicated, but I’ll leave it for Matthew to answer if they are considering to support GLM 5.3 Flash using the same idea. On the other hand, their repo already has a GLM 5.3 Flash support that was referenced in this thread GLM-5.3-Flash: 320B total parameters / 18B active - #597 by ekkis

The numbers seem to have improved a lot since then even for TP2 GitHub - kindlingai/glm-5.3-flash-gx10: GLM-5.3-Flash (NVFP4) at TP=4 across 4x ASUS GX10 / GB10 - vLLM + mentat instead of Ray, 524k context, DFlash2. Minimal working recipe. · GitHub

Having the above squared away, and without polluting this GLM 5.3 Flash thread with too much GLM 5.3 numbers, here is my experience that’s relevant to this thread:

  1. The engine (gr8) itself is in beta release, and it does not support TC-45 (tool-choice) and TC-64 (response_format “json_schema”), where engine endpoint responded HTTP 400 before reaching the model, so those were excluded from tool-eval-bench scoring. With that, 4 standard (seed 42, hardmode, etc) trials were run, and the scores are 91/92/91/90. While these numbers look underwhelming for a full GLM 5.3 model (versus what we get from technigmaai flash counterpart), I suspect it has something to do with the engine’s JSON support. There were at least 4 failed/partial cases with “correctly called xxxx but output is not valid JSON”. So, don’t discredit GLM 5.3 for its Flash sibling yet.

  2. GSM8K is 96.29% (1270/1319), zero-shot, temperatur 0, low reasoning. I don’t have a matching GLM 5.3 Flash config to compare to. Previously, I was getting 97.3% with technigmaai GLM 5.3 Flash stack with 8-shot prompting.

  3. I was gladly surprised by its decode and prefill speed for the full model. Single-request decode is approximately 33.7-37.4 tok/s across 0-64K contexts. Prefill is 1,389 tok/s at 16k, 1,328 at 64K and1,164 at 128K. (head node GPU clock capped at 2200 MHz). technigmaai GLM 5.3 Flash has a lot faster decode and prefills for sure (which is my current prod).

gr8 image is very small (2.81 GB), but I have not measured its runtime memory footprint that many memory-constrained users may be interested in. and, this is the only engine that I needed to cap my GX10 GPU clock to 2200 MHz without getting my head node to shutdown (twice). Overall, I think gr8 is a promising full-model (GLM 5.3) serving stack, but not yet a proven drop-in production replacement. I am looking forward to its full release (i.e., out of beta).

posts.cooked:
@eugr_nv For a four spark cluster, would you recommend this new quantization over NVIDIA’s previous one?

huggingface.co

nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local · Hugging Face

We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.

huggingface.co

nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4 · Hugging Face

We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.

I’ve been using the latter with great results using your spark-vllm-docker (2026-10-10 version most recently) with a customized YAML for adaptive MTP (DFlash2 also works in my testing based on a separate YAML). This config provides concurrency up to about 7 instances at 1M context:

# NVIDIA GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 on four DGX Sparks, launched with sparkrun.
# Requires the candidate image tag and refreshed model snapshot on all nodes.
# Native adaptive MTP: starts at K3, adapts within K1-K5, window 32.

recipe_version: "2"

model: nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4
container: glm53-b12x:candidate-2026-10-10
runtime: vllm-distributed

min_nodes: 4
max_nodes: 4

metadata:
  description: NVIDIA GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 on four DGX Sparks with native adaptive MTP K1-K5 and initial K3

mods:
  - mods/drop-caches

defaults:
  port: 8000
  host: 0.0.0.0
  tensor_parallel: 4
  pipeline_parallel: 1
  decode_context_parallel: 1
  block_size: 256
  max_model_len: 1048576
  max_num_seqs: 8
  max_num_batched_tokens: 8192
  max_cudagraph_capture_size: 64
  gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90

  # Initial K3 is a starting value, not a minimum.
  speculative_config: >-
    {"method":"mtp",
    "num_speculative_tokens":5,
    "adaptive_speculative_tokens_window":32,
    "adaptive_speculative_tokens_initial":3,
    "moe_backend":"auto",
    "attention_backend":"B12X"}

env:
  NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS: "4"
  NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS: "4"
  CUTE_DSL_ARCH: "sm_121a"
  VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD: "spawn"
  VLLM_ENABLE_ROCE_ALLREDUCE: "1"

command: |
  vllm serve nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4 \
    --host {host} \
    --port {port} \
    --distributed-executor-backend mp \
    --tensor-parallel-size {tensor_parallel} \
    --pipeline-parallel-size {pipeline_parallel} \
    --decode-context-parallel-size {decode_context_parallel} \
    --load-format fastsafetensors \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
    --attention-backend B12X \
    --block-size {block_size} \
    --moe-backend b12x \
    --linear-backend b12x \
    --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune \
    --mamba-cache-mode align \
    --enable-prefix-caching \
    --enable-chunked-prefill \
    --max-model-len {max_model_len} \
    --max-num-seqs {max_num_seqs} \
    --max-num-batched-tokens {max_num_batched_tokens} \
    --max-cudagraph-capture-size {max_cudagraph_capture_size} \
    --speculative-config '{speculative_config}' \
    --reasoning-parser glm45 \
    --tool-call-parser glm47 \
    --enable-auto-tool-choice \
    --gpu-memory-utilization {gpu_memory_utilization}

Thanks for the quick reply! By the by, I see a goal with this new quant was increasing the KV cache pool for 2x Spark by shrinking the weights while retaining as much quality as possible. While it may not be a current goal, it would be amazing to have an FP4-Local variant of GLM-5.3 (non-Flash) in addition to this one:

While I appreciate this model exists, unfortunately it’s just too large to squeeze into 4x Sparks, meaning an Int4-Int8Mix (e.g., Tech2wild/GLM-5.3-Int4-Int8Mix · Hugging Face) is the only real viable option to hit 1M context with DCP4. It would be amazing to have an official NVIDIA image of the full 5.3 model that can fit into a mid-size Spark cluster.

(At the same time, I can totally see why 2x Spark is likely the priority, and I am grateful for everything you, Luke, and others do for the community in general. It’s also possible that the FP4-Local version of GLM 5.3 wouldn’t hit the 400GB ballpark, but I’m just guesstimating a ballpark possibility here: 178/204 [proportional savings across the two GLM-5.3 Flash quants] * 465 [the existing NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 version] = 405)

posts.name: Matthew
posts.cooked:
Check out the troubleshooting section on GitHub - kindlingai/glm-5.3-flash-gx10: GLM-5.3-Flash (NVFP4) at TP=4 across 4x ASUS GX10 / GB10 - vLLM + mentat instead of Ray, 524k context, DFlash2. Minimal working recipe. · GitHub - that sounds like this:

Prefill at half speed, every metric healthy. If NCCL all-reduce crawls (~12 Gb/s) while ib_write_bw reads a healthy 109 Gb/s and no error counter moves, the ConnectX-7 has latched a slow fallback state from the DAC cables being hot-plugged. Power off and unplug for a minute: a reboot does not clear it, and neither does a NIC hotplug reset. The tell is that NCCL Tree beats Ring. Healthy on both roots is Ring 180-191 Gb/s against Tree 55-93 (NOTES.md). A single unidirectional stream cannot see this, which is why the RDMA test passes; a ring collective, sending and receiving at once, can.

This applies to more that just this recipe. It’s unfortunately just something that happens, sometimes with cable replugs, sometimes just a brownout.

Yeah I gave this some benefit of the doubt, and as my nodes were idle, in between tasks, I shut both down and left them unplugged for a few mins.

They are back up and running their usual model at the same speed, not sure whether knapcio is going to improve things given my recipe was running at the same speed before the reboot…
